text.p: Kingstream Resources NL is on track to begin construction of its $1.2 billion to A$1.4 billion steel project in Western Australia in the third quarter of this year, Kingstream's managing director Nick Zuks said on Tuesday.

In an interview with Reuters, Zuks said the due diligence required as part of the planned merger with Taiwan's An Feng Steel Co Ltd had been completed and Kingstream was now awaiting the independent expert's report from Grant Samuel.
"The timetable is for the shareholders to vote (on the merger) by the end of March or early April," Zuks said.
The merged An Feng and Kingstream plan to develop the Midwest iron and steel project with annual capacity of 2.4 million tonnes of steel slab near the port of Geraldton, north of Perth.
"We still need FIRB (Foreign Investment Review Board approval, and the Consultative Environmental Revew for the plant site will be released shortly," Zuks said.
"The main approval we are seeking at the moment is from (the Western Australian) Cabinet in relation to the state agreement and we expect that next week." he said.
"The financing of the project is an on-going process. We have had a lot of interest from various banks and the startup for the construction is on track for the third quarter."

Zuks spoke to Reuters following renewed interest in the status of the Kingstream project after the announcement on Sunday by the U.S.-owned gas pipeline group PGT Australia Pty Ltd that it had applied for approval to build a second Dampier-to-Bunbury natural gas pipeline in Western Australia.
PGT is a subsidiary of Pacific Gas & Electric Corp.
The PGT announcement met with a cool response from the state Minister for Resources Development and Energy, Colin Barnett, who described it as "most unusual" and "provocative".

The government made plain it believed a second 1,600 km pipeline for offshore gas from the port of Dampier in the state's northwest to Bunbury in the southwest would sharply devalue the existing state-owned pipeline that it wants to privatise.
Zuks declined to comment on Barnett's response but said the existing pipeline did not have the capacity to supply the Kingstream project.
"It's at full capacity at the moment," Zuks said.
"It needs either looping or a new pipeline to cater for us."
Zuks also said PGT Australia had tendered to supply gas to the Kingstream project and was one of the three remaining bidders.
"We expect to name the winning tenderer at the end of this month," Zuks said.
